# Preface {.unnumbered}

You have just spent weeks learning how your own cells work: membranes, organelles, the electron
transport chain, the path from DNA to protein. This book uses that knowledge from the first page. A
microbe faces many of the problems your cells face: it needs a boundary, a source of energy and a way
to copy itself. Its solutions differ from yours, and drugs and the immune system act on those
differences.

Microbiology is often taught as a long sequence of organisms, each with its own list of facts. The
2026 revision of the microbiology core knowledge objectives for medical schools recommends moving away
from that approach [@bauler2026objectives]. This book instead asks the same six questions of every
kind of microbe, starting with what it is built from and ending with what it has that your cells lack.
[*The microbial world*](chapters/principles/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-questions) sets out the six
questions. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites answer them differently, and later chapters use
those answers to explain how each group causes disease and how it is detected and controlled.

## What the book covers

The book has two parts. Part I, *Principles*, builds a toolkit: how microbes are built, how they obtain
energy and change, how they cause harm and spread, and how they are detected and controlled. Part II,
*Meeting the microbes*, takes each group of organisms in turn and asks the six questions of it.

The book leaves out where each infection occurs in the body, how it is diagnosed and how it is
treated, because you will meet those in the organ-system blocks, and pharmacology will teach the drugs.
The aim here is a framework that makes those later facts easier to place. A named organism appears as
an example of a trait, and organisms usually appear in contrasting pairs, because students who compare
two cases side by side apply the principle to new cases more often than students who study each case
alone [@alfieri2013contrasting].

Each technical term is defined where it first appears in a chapter, and all of them are collected in
the [glossary](glossary.qmd).

## How to use the interactive parts

| Activity | What you do |
|---|---|
| Predict, then reveal | Commit to a prediction before the answer appears. Guess even when unsure: a wrong prediction followed by feedback still helps you learn |
| Contrast pairs | Find the one feature that separates two similar organisms, then sort descriptions between them |
| Check your understanding | Answer a short quiz at the end of each chapter. Most questions ask why something happens |
| Flashcards | Review the chapter's ideas over the following weeks; the deck spaces each card further apart as you get it right |
| Practise | Work through a short branching case using the chapter's ideas |

Your answers are saved only in your own browser. Nothing is sent anywhere, and there is no login.
